_comment: Mutation survivors accepted as a baseline for the binding sweep (the membership walk, the context it carries, and the frontend). The nightly ratchet fails when a survivor appears outside this set, and when an entry is no longer a survivor. Regenerate with `python scripts/mutation_gate.py --baseline walk --update` after a sweep, and only ever let this set shrink. Entries are the survivor line without its line:col position, so they survive unrelated code motion.

_accepted.crates/valgebra-py/src/build/classes.rs:: The guard `!origin.is_instance_of::<PyType>()` keeps a class origin from asking the `typing_extensions` table, and the mutant asks it for a class and skips it for a form. On the interpreter this sweep runs, 3.12 with `typing_extensions` installed from the lock, that module's `Required` and `NotRequired` are `typing`'s own objects, from 3.11 on, and the loop above has already matched them: the table answers `false` for every origin that reaches the guard, on either side of it, and the mutant moves cost alone. So the frontend's arms for that module's own objects answer what the `typing` arms already answered, and a mutant of them moves nothing a test can read. They answer where the module defines objects of its own -- 3.10, or the stand-in `a_typing_extensions_form_reads_as_its_typing_spelling` installs on an interpreter that cannot import the module, which is where that corpus row kills this mutant. The arm dies with the 3.10 floor.
_accepted.crates/valgebra-py/src/build/generics.rs: `is_extension(any) || is_extension(never)` becomes `is_extension(any) && is_extension(never)`, and no object is both. On the interpreter this sweep runs, 3.12 with `typing_extensions` installed from the lock, that module's `Any` and `Never` are `typing`'s own objects, from 3.11 on, which `refuse_literal_form` has already compared by identity before it asks this, so both read `false` for any argument that reaches them and either spelling reads `false`. So the arms for that module's own objects answer what the `typing` arms already answered, and a mutant of them moves nothing a test can read. They answer where the module defines objects of its own -- 3.10, or the stand-in `a_typing_extensions_form_reads_as_its_typing_spelling` installs on an interpreter that cannot import the module, which is where that corpus row kills this mutant. The two arms die with the 3.10 floor.

`required || not_required || read_only` over the `typing_extensions` table becomes `(required && not_required) || read_only`. On the interpreter this sweep runs, 3.12 with `typing_extensions` installed from the lock, the first two are `typing`'s own objects, from 3.11 on, which the loop above has already compared, so both read `false` for any origin that reaches them and either spelling reads `read_only` alone: `ReadOnly`, the qualifier 3.12's `typing` lacks, is read the same way. So the frontend's arms for that module's own objects answer what the `typing` arms already answered, and a mutant of them moves nothing a test can read. They answer where the module defines objects of its own -- 3.10, or the stand-in `a_typing_extensions_form_reads_as_its_typing_spelling` installs on an interpreter that cannot import the module, which is where that corpus row kills this mutant. The two arms die with the 3.10 floor.

`typing`'s `Unpack` or `typing_extensions`' becomes `typing`'s and `typing_extensions`'. On the interpreter this sweep runs, 3.12 with `typing_extensions` installed from the lock, the two are one object, from 3.12 on, so each side is the same comparison and `a || a` is `a && a`. So the frontend's arms for that module's own objects answer what the `typing` arms already answered, and a mutant of them moves nothing a test can read. They answer where the module defines objects of its own -- 3.10, or the stand-in `a_typing_extensions_form_reads_as_its_typing_spelling` installs on an interpreter that cannot import the module, which is where that corpus row kills this mutant. 3.11 is such a release for `Unpack`, so this arm outlives the 3.10 floor by one release.

So a mutant of the mask can only move cost, which is `scripts/perf_gate.py --binding-annotated`'s business and not a test's. _accepted.crates/valgebra-py/src/check/index.rs: d: `if !fields.is_empty()` read as `if fields.is_empty()`: an attribute record with no fields gains a plan of no names, and one with fields gains none. Both halves are cost. A plan of no names is what a record of no fields would get anyway, and a record with fields falls back to its own text. The walk falls back for a schema the index does not carry -- every plan lookup in `check/walk/` is `Option`-shaped with the fallback written beside it -- so a traversal that skips a node decides the same values and only pays more for them.

The attribute plan, which holds each declared name interned. Without it `attr_record_matches` reads `field.name` and interns nothing, so every attribute lookup hashes the name rather than comparing a pointer -- the same answer from the same names. The walk falls back for a schema the index does not carry -- every plan lookup in `check/walk/` is `Option`-shaped with the fallback written beside it -- so a traversal that skips a node decides the same values and only pays more for them.

Descent only, as the intersection arm above: neither node carries a plan, and the arm reaches what is inside them. Accepting a cost-only survivor is honest only where something counts the cost; that shape is what counts this one. _accepted.crates/valgebra-py/src/check/index.rs: r: The traversal `__traverse__` hands the cycle collector. Every object it yields is an interned `str`, and a `str` refers to nothing, so it can be no edge of a cycle and a collector that never sees one still collects correctly. The method exists because a traversal omitting an owned reference is wrong on its own terms, not because this omission leaks: no test can distinguish the two, and none should be written to.
_accepted.crates/valgebra-py/src/check/walk/record: Cannot change a report. The counter it disables is what lets a closed record holding exactly its own keys skip a scan that would find nothing: stuck at zero, the count matches only an empty value, so every other record falls through to the scan and the scan reports what the count would have. Only the cost moves, and cost is the instruction budget's business. The other half of the same condition is not equivalent and is killed by tests/test_mutation.py: a value that grows while it is explained leaves the count matching entries it no longer has, which is why the length is read again before the skip is taken.

`undeclared == Undeclared::Read || plan.keys.len() != fields.len()` weakened to `&&`: a record whose clause reads an undeclared key's value, with a complete plan, is read by its keys before the scan, which it is handed to wherever every declared field holds, since its keys alone do not settle it. The answers are the scan's on either side. What moves is the order a refusal is reached in: read by its keys, a field decided by its own value is read before the fields declared ahead of it, so a predicate in one of those does not run where the tag refuses -- which the scan, reading the dict's order, may run. A test that kills this mutant pins the scan to the dearer order, which no page promises.
_accepted.crates/valgebra-py/src/check/walk/scalar: The mutant's body is the function's own: the error is a parameter, and a parameter is dropped where its function returns, so `()` drops it at the very place `drop(err)` does -- inside `set_aside`, out of line, which is the whole of what the function is for. Inlined into `check_refine`'s loop over its constraints, the drop's read of whether the thread is attached has its thread-local address taken ahead of the loop, once for every refined value; out of line, it is taken only where the error a string holding a lone surrogate raises is dropped. The original and the mutant compile to the same function, so neither a test nor a count can tell them apart.
